displayQuote: Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough

meta.title: Who really said "Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Elon Musk. He said it to Fast Company in the February 2005 article "Hondas in Space," contrasting SpaceX with what he called a silly NASA notion.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Musk, on the record: Fast Company, "Hondas in Space" (Feb 2005). The full line opens with a jab at NASA that most quote lists drop.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Musk said it to Fast Company writer Jennifer Reingold, in “Hondas in Space” (published 1 February 2005). The article quotes it directly, right after the set-up “There’s a silly notion that failure’s not an option at NASA.” The wording is confirmed against the article text.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Direct quotation from Musk in a magazine profile of SpaceX

source.excerpt: Getting something out there fast inevitably leads to failures — but that’s to be expected at SpaceX. When something goes wrong, “first of all, there’s a good lashing,” jokes Musk. Getting serious, he says, “There’s a silly notion that failure’s not an option at NASA. Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough.” In fact, says Kevin Brogan, a senior design engineer, “the first time we had a major engine failure Elon was kind of excited. It gave him some street cred.”
trail: Fast Company quotes Musk word for word in Jennifer Reingold’s SpaceX profile “Hondas in Space” (published 1 February 2005) ↗.
Wikiquote’s sourced Elon Musk page ↗ lists the line under 2005 and cites the same Fast Company article, but its transcription has a typo (“aren’t not failing”).
Quote roundups pass it around without a source. Wikiquote’s talk page ↗ lists it under “Further unsourced quotes,” and the only source given there is an Inc. listicle.
source.excerptNote: Most quote lists leave out Musk’s opening sentence, a jab at NASA’s “failure’s not an option” motto. Without it, “here” has nothing to point to: it means SpaceX, as opposed to NASA.
source.rightsNote: The line first appeared in print in Fast Company’s February 2005 article “Hondas in Space.” A 2005 publication is still under US copyright. The site’s footer names Mansueto Ventures, LLC as the copyright holder. Quoting two sentences with attribution, as this page does, is ordinary fair-use quotation.

author.bio: Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 and is its CEO and chief engineer. He also leads Tesla. When Fast Company profiled SpaceX in early 2005, the company was still developing its first rocket, the Falcon I, and Musk made the case for building fast, testing hard and treating failures as part of the process.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, garbled history
misattribution.intro: Musk really did say this. What goes wrong online is the setting, the wording and the missing NASA set-up.

items.why: 24/7 Wall St (Feb 2025) ↗ says Musk said it “during a SpaceX Q&A session” and gives no date. The documented source is a 2005 Fast Company magazine profile.

items.who: “If you’re not failing, you’re not taking enough risks”
items.why: The same 24/7 Wall St article ↗ rewrites the second sentence in its headline. Musk said “innovating enough,” not “taking enough risks.”
Articles such as CleanTechnica (2020) ↗ repeat the line with no venue or year. Wikiquote’s talk page ↗ files it under “Further unsourced quotes,” citing only an Inc. roundup.
Wikiquote’s main Musk page ↗ cites the right article but transcribes it with a double negative. The article itself ↗ reads “If things are not failing.”

misattribution.truthLine: The documented source is Fast Company, “Hondas in Space” (1 February 2005) ↗: “There’s a silly notion that failure’s not an option at NASA. Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough.”

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: The line is a reply to a famous slogan. “Failure is not an option” is a motto tied to NASA’s mission control. Musk calls it “a silly notion” and offers SpaceX’s opposite: break things early and often, because a test that never fails isn’t pushing hard enough.

In the Fast Company profile, the remark sits in a passage about SpaceX’s build-fast, “test the crap out of it” approach while developing the Falcon I. An engineer recalls that after the first major engine failure, “Elon was kind of excited.” Musk’s reply: “If I had the option of not having it blow up, I’d rather not. But it was pretty cool.”
context.pull: There’s a silly notion that failure’s not an option at NASA.

sourcesVerified.claim: Fast Company's 'Hondas in Space' by Jennifer Reingold (datePublished 2005-02-01, February 2005 / Issue 91) quotes Musk: 'There's a silly notion that failure's not an option at NASA. Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough.' Footer copyright: Mansueto Ventures, LLC.
Wikiquote's Elon Musk page lists the line under 2005, citing Fast Company 'Hondas in Space' (1 February 2005), transcribed as 'If things aren't not failing'; no Misattributed section.
Wikiquote's Talk:Elon_Musk lists 'Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough.' under 'Further unsourced quotes', citing an Inc.com roundup.
24/7 Wall St (John Seetoo, 24 Feb 2025) says Musk said it 'during a SpaceX Q&A session' with no date; its headline rewords the line as 'If you're not failing, you're not taking enough risks'.
CleanTechnica (Matt Pressman, 1 Feb 2020) repeats the quote without a venue or year.
Musk was born June 28, 1971, and founded SpaceX in 2002, where he is founder, CEO and chief engineer.
